title: Male obesity: what it means for your health. What to do next.
seoTitle: Male Obesity: BMI, Waist and Your First Health Check
description: Obese or not sure? What BMI and waist mean for men, who gets a free NHS Health Check, and checks for under-40s and over-74s.
intro: Short answer: if your BMI or waist suggests obesity, the most useful first step is a proper check of your blood pressure and heart and diabetes risk. In England, men aged 40 to 74 without certain existing conditions can get a free NHS Health Check. Younger or older men have other routes, set out below.
html:
Male obesity: which health check should a man get first?

Short answer: if your BMI or waist suggests obesity, the most useful first step is a proper check of your blood pressure and heart and diabetes risk. In England, men aged 40 to 74 without certain existing conditions can get a free NHS Health Check. Younger or older men have other routes, set out below.

What does this mean for me as a man?

It means the number on the scales is a prompt, not a verdict. Carrying extra weight, especially around the middle, can raise blood pressure and the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease and stroke, often with no symptoms at all. You can feel fine and still not know. A check turns guessing into something you can act on, and it does not commit you to anything.

Am I eligible for a free NHS Health Check?

The NHS Health Check is for adults in England aged 40 to 74. It is not offered if you already have certain conditions, including heart disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, high blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, a previous stroke or mini-stroke, heart failure, peripheral arterial disease or inherited high cholesterol, or if you are already prescribed a statin. If you have one of those conditions, you should be getting regular check-ups through your care team instead.

You should be invited every five years by your GP or local council. If you think you are eligible and have not been invited, contact your GP practice. If your practice does not offer it, your local council can tell you where to book. The check usually takes 20 to 30 minutes and covers your height, weight, blood pressure and a blood test.

What if I'm under 40, over 74, or not eligible?

No man needs to be left out. Here are the routes the NHS describes:

  • Under 40: ask your GP practice or a pharmacist about checking your blood pressure and weight-related risk, especially if heart disease or diabetes runs in your family.
  • Blood pressure at a pharmacy: the NHS advises getting your blood pressure checked at a pharmacy or GP surgery if you think you might be at risk, or if you are 40 or over and have not had it checked for more than five years. Many pharmacies offer this, though some may charge, so ask first. Read our blood pressure guide.
  • 75 and over: speak to your GP practice, who can look at your heart, blood pressure and diabetes risk as part of your usual care.
  • Already diagnosed with a condition: keep up your regular reviews and raise your weight at your next one.
  • Private blood tests: these are an option if you want extra detail, but they do not replace NHS care. Take any result to your GP. See our information about private health checks.

What should I do if I have worrying symptoms?

Do not wait for a routine check. Call 999 for chest pain, signs of a stroke such as a face drooping on one side, arm weakness or slurred speech, or severe difficulty breathing. For symptoms that worry you but are not an emergency, use NHS 111 online, call 111 or contact your GP practice.

From Matt

"I'm not a doctor. My own experience explains why I care about this; it doesn't tell us what's causing your symptoms. I wasn't just carrying extra weight. I was carrying blood pressure, a bad knee, a drinking habit, a bad mood, grief and a fright, all at once. Maybe for you it's the belt that's run out of holes. You might just be tired of being tired. That is enough reason to take yourself seriously."

What can I usefully do next?

Measure your waist and check your BMI using the tools on this page, then write the numbers down. If you are 40 to 74 in England, check whether you are due an NHS Health Check. If not, use one of the routes above. Take your numbers to the appointment, along with anything that has changed: sleep, snoring, energy or mood.

Frequently asked questions

Is the NHS Health Check free?

Yes. In England it is free for eligible adults aged 40 to 74 who do not already have certain heart, kidney, diabetes or blood pressure conditions.

How often can I have an NHS Health Check?

If you are eligible, you should be invited every five years by your GP practice or local council.

Can I get my blood pressure checked without seeing a GP?

Yes. Many pharmacies offer blood pressure checks. Some may charge, so ask first.

I'm 35 and overweight. What should I do?

Ask your GP practice or a pharmacist about a blood pressure check and your risk, especially if heart disease or diabetes runs in your family.

  • NHS: when to use 111
  • NICE: overweight and obesity management

title: Men's health MOT: what's checked and is it worth it?
seoTitle: Men's Health MOT: What's Checked and Is It Worth It?
description: What a men's health MOT checks, who gets a free NHS Health Check, routes for under-40s and over-74s, and when a private MOT is worth it.
intro: A men's health MOT is a check-up of your heart, blood vessels and metabolic health. The free NHS Health Check, for eligible men aged 40 to 74 in England, measures your weight, waist and blood pressure, checks cholesterol and sometimes blood sugar, then gives you a 10-year risk score. Private MOTs add more tests, but more is not always better.
html:
A men's health MOT is a check-up of your heart, blood vessels and metabolic health. The free NHS Health Check, for eligible men aged 40 to 74 in England, measures your weight, waist and blood pressure, checks cholesterol and sometimes blood sugar, then gives you a 10-year risk score. Private MOTs add more tests, but more is not always better.

Our health MOT hub covers SHIFT's own route. This guide covers what is checked, who gets it free, and when paying makes sense.

What does this mean for me as a man?

High blood pressure and high cholesterol usually have no symptoms, so feeling fine tells you very little. A check turns guesswork into numbers you can act on.

What does the NHS Health Check include?

It takes about 20 to 30 minutes, usually with a pharmacist, nurse or healthcare assistant. It usually includes:

  • your height, weight and waist
  • a blood pressure test
  • a cholesterol test, and possibly a blood sugar test
  • questions about family history, smoking, drinking and how active you are

You get a risk score for heart and circulation problems over the next 10 years, plus your BMI, blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes risk, then talk through what to change.

Who can get one free, and what if I'm not eligible?

The NHS Health Check is for people aged 40 to 74 in England who do not already have conditions such as heart disease, diabetes, kidney disease, high blood pressure, atrial fibrillation or a previous stroke, and who are not already on statins. If that is you, you should be invited every five years. Not been invited? Contact your GP practice, or your local council if the practice does not offer it.

Outside that group, you still have a route:

  • Under 40: ask your GP practice or a pharmacist about a blood pressure check, especially if heart problems run in your family. Some pharmacies charge, so ask first.
  • 40 or over: you may be eligible for a free NHS pharmacy blood pressure check, even between invitations. Ask the pharmacy about eligibility.
  • 75 or over: the NHS Health Check stops, but your GP practice can still check your blood pressure, weight and risk. Ask.
  • Already diagnosed: your care team should review you regularly instead. Chase it if not.
  • Any age: you can choose a private blood test or health check, as long as you know what you are buying.

If you live in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, ask your GP practice or pharmacy what is offered locally.

Is a private health MOT worth it?

Sometimes. Private MOTs can add liver, kidney and thyroid tests, hormones and more, which helps when you have a specific question. But more markers is not a better check. The UK National Screening Committee warns private screening can bring false alarms, false reassurance and tests the NHS may need to repeat.

Before you book, the government's guidance suggests asking:

  • Is this already offered free on the NHS?
  • Is the provider registered with the Care Quality Commission?
  • What do the fees cover, and will follow-up cost extra?
  • What happens if a result is unclear or out of range?

If you have symptoms, see your GP. Screening is not for symptoms.

When should I get help straight away?

Do not wait for an MOT. Call 999 for chest pain that does not go away, signs of a stroke or severe difficulty breathing. Use NHS 111 for chest pain that comes and goes, or frequent headaches or blurred vision.

From Matt

"I'm not a doctor. It wasn't one moment for me. It was a pile of them, and I'd got very good at stepping round it. Getting a grip included accepting help. I didn't do it all by sheer force of personality."

What can I usefully do next?

Measure your waist and check your BMI with our free tools, and write the numbers down. Book the right check for your age from the list above, and take one question you want answered. Afterwards, our guide to understanding results helps you read your blood tests.

Frequently asked questions

Is the NHS Health Check the same as a health MOT?

It is the NHS version. Private MOTs often add tests, but the NHS check covers the core heart and diabetes risks, with advice.

Does a health MOT check testosterone or PSA?

The NHS Health Check does not. Some private checks do. If you have symptoms or worries about either, talk to your GP rather than relying on a bundled test.

I'm 35. Can I get a health check?

Not the NHS Health Check, but you can ask your GP practice or a pharmacist about a blood pressure check and your risk.

Ready for one useful step? Use Start Here to plan yours. It's free, and you don't need to buy anything.

  • UK National Screening Committee: NHS and commercial screening
  • NHS: when to call 999

title: Testosterone and weight: which comes first?
seoTitle: Does Weight Gain Lower Testosterone in Men? | Shift Some Timber
description: Weight gain and low testosterone can feed each other. Learn why symptoms are not a diagnosis, what weight loss may do, and when to see your GP.
intro: Short answer: yes, weight gain can be linked with lower testosterone, and the link can run both ways. Carrying more body fat is associated with lower measured testosterone in many men, and low testosterone can in turn affect muscle, energy and body composition. Which came first is not something you can work out from symptoms or an online quiz. It needs a proper conversation with a GP, an examination and correctly timed blood tests.
html:
Short answer: yes, weight gain can be linked with lower testosterone, and the link can run both ways. Carrying more body fat is associated with lower measured testosterone in many men, and low testosterone can in turn affect muscle, energy and body composition. Which came first is not something you can work out from symptoms or an online quiz. It needs a proper conversation with a GP, an examination and correctly timed blood tests.

Why it works in both directions

European andrology guidelines describe a pattern called functional hypogonadism, where lower testosterone happens alongside other conditions rather than a problem with the testes or pituitary gland itself. Obesity is one of the main conditions they discuss, along with type 2 diabetes, poor sleep, heavy drinking, some medicines and long-term illness (Corona et al., 2020).

In plain terms, extra body fat, especially around the middle, can change how hormones are made and used. Lower testosterone may then make it harder to hold on to muscle and easier to feel flat and tired. That can feed into eating more, moving less and sleeping worse. It is a loop, not a straight line.

Why symptoms alone are not enough

Tiredness, low mood, poorer sleep, reduced sex drive and a softer middle are common. They can be connected to testosterone, but they can also come from sleep problems such as sleep apnoea, thyroid issues, depression, diabetes, stress, alcohol or medicines.

That is why the guidelines stress repeated morning blood tests and a look at the wider health picture before anyone talks about treatment. Our guide to testosterone and energy goes into the symptoms in more detail.

What weight loss may do

The same guidelines suggest that for men with functional hypogonadism linked to excess weight, the first step is usually to address the underlying cause, including weight, activity, sleep and alcohol. Some men living with male obesity see their testosterone levels improve after meaningful weight loss. The response varies, and an improvement does not prove that weight was the only issue.

Things that support the basics:

  • regular strength and everyday activity
  • enough protein and a pattern of eating you can keep up
  • steady sleep and less alcohol
  • getting persistent symptoms checked rather than guessing

Supplements sold as testosterone boosters are not a substitute for assessment.

Where testosterone treatment fits

Testosterone treatment is a prescription-only medicine with specific uses, risks and monitoring needs, not an energy product. Whether it is appropriate is a decision for a qualified clinician, based on confirmed blood results and your overall health. This article is general information and does not recommend any treatment.

From Matt

"Nor should you silently file every symptom under 'it must be my weight.' Persistent fatigue, disrupted sleep, pain, marked breathlessness or changes that worry you deserve attention in their own right. A GP can take a history and decide what assessment is appropriate."

If you have been putting off that appointment, Matt suggests you do not need a polished speech. Something like: "I want to talk about my weight and general health. My energy has changed, and I would like to understand my options."

Source: Matt O'Brien, Shift Some Timber book draft (manuscript, 2026). Matt lost around 4½ stone over about eleven months through changes to eating, movement and prescribed weight-loss treatment after a clinical assessment (Matt's author profile, shiftsometimber.co.uk). That is his experience, not a promise of results, and he is not a clinician.

When to get help

  • Routine: persistent tiredness, low sex drive, reduced morning erections or mood changes. Book a GP appointment.
  • Not sure how urgent it is: contact NHS 111 online or by phone.
  • Emergency: chest pain, severe breathlessness, signs of a stroke or immediate danger of serious self-harm. Call 999 or go to A&E.

This applies to men of any age. Hormone and weight questions are not only for older men.

Track energy/sleep in My Timber

Track energy/sleep in My Timber alongside your food and movement, then take what you notice to your appointment. Diagnosis and treatment decisions stay with your healthcare professional.

Frequently asked questions

Does belly fat lower testosterone?

Higher body fat, particularly around the waist, is associated with lower testosterone measures in many men. The relationship is complex and needs proper assessment.

Will losing weight raise my testosterone?

It may improve levels in some men living with obesity, but results vary and symptoms can have other causes.

Can low testosterone make you put on weight?

It can affect muscle and body composition, which may make weight gain easier.

Can I test testosterone at home?

Home kits exist, but a single result is hard to interpret. Guidelines recommend repeated morning blood tests reviewed by a clinician.

If you need urgent mental health help and are not in immediate danger, call NHS 111 and select the mental health option, or ask your GP for an urgent appointment.

Sources

  • European Academy of Andrology: functional hypogonadism guideline (Corona et al., 2020)
  • NICE: overweight and obesity management
  • NHS: obesity
  • NHS: adult physical activity guidance
  • NHS: urgent mental health help
